title: Dust aerosol properties and radiative effects over the global oceans from synergistic spaceborne observations and modeling
abstract: The microphysical and radiative properties of mineral dust aerosols, a major species of atmospheric aerosols, are fundamental to quantifying broad dust aerosol impacts. At present, substantial uncertainties remain in estimating dust microphysical properties and radiative effects on a global scale, stemming from source-dependent mineralogical variability that leads to substantial varaiations in dust optical and microphysical properties, as well as inconsistencies in the physical assumptions adopted in spaceborne retrievals and radiative transfer simulations. This study develops a physically consistent approach for retrieving dust aerosol properties over the global oceans and to quantify the associated radiative effects through the synergistic use of collocated observations made by the Cloud-Aerosol Lidar with Orthogonal Polarization (CALIOP) and the Infrared Imaging Radiometer (IIR) aboard the Cloud-Aerosol Lidar and Infrared Pathfinder Satellite Observations (CALIPSO) platform. The new retrieval algorithm uses the TAMUdust2020 dust single-scattering property database, which represents dust in terms of an ensemble of randomly distorted hexahedral particles, and incorporates a region- and mineralogy-dependent refractive index dataset, and avoids an empirical lidar-ratio assumption. The retrieved dust properties are incorporated into a dust optical property parameterization for the Rapid Radiative Transfer Model for Global Climate Models (RRTMG), ensuring that a consistent representation of dust optical and microphysical properties is used for both the retrieval implementation and downstream radiative transfer calculations. To quantify the influence of regional mineralogical variability and longwave scattering on the simulated radiative effects, this study also presents the global and seasonal distributions of dust aerosol optical thickness, effective particle radius, vertical structure, and associated radiative effects over the global oceans. The present findings show that dust exerts shortwave (SW) cooling and longwave (LW) warming over the global oceans, with area-weighted annual mean SW/LW effects of −1.358/+0.329 W m −2 at the surface and − 0.796/+0.029 W m −2 at the top of the atmosphere, respectively.

title: Development and validation of a red-edge-based index for improving satellite detection of algal blooms in inland waters
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: The increasing frequency of freshwater algal blooms threatens aquatic ecosystems globally. While remote sensing algorithms are widely used for bloom detection, conventional methods frequently exhibit degraded performance under optically complex conditions (e.g., sunglint, thin clouds, and high turbidity) and lack sensitivity to sparse blooms. To address these limitations, this study introduces the Red-Edge Floating Algae Index (RFAI). Structured as a baseline-height model, the RFAI mathematically isolates the scattering-induced spectral curvature of algal blooms using three critical Sentinel-2 Multispectral Instrument (MSI) bands: the green reflectance peak (∼560 nm), the red absorption trough (∼665 nm), and the red-edge reflectance peak (∼704 nm). This formulation effectively decouples genuine target signals from confounding background noise. Comparative validation against 17 widely used indices across a diverse set of inland lakes demonstrated the statistically significant overall effectiveness of the RFAI ( p < 0.0001), yielding precision and F1-score improvements of up to 42.8 % and 26.6 %, respectively, under locally optimized parameterizations. Crucially, the RFAI demonstrates robust comprehensive stability across highly variable, optically challenging conditions, effectively mitigating the severe performance fluctuations often observed in individual conventional indices. Supported by a novel optical-type-stratified thresholding strategy, the RFAI establishes a scalable and versatile framework for operational bloom monitoring using compatible red-edge satellite systems, enabling the generation of reliable observational records essential for the sustainable management of aquatic ecosystems.

title: Reconstructing multi-temporal Glacier area changes to improve mass balance estimates in the Southeastern Tibetan Plateau (2000–2025)
abstract: The southeastern Tibetan Plateau (SETP), a critical component of the “Asian Water Tower”, hosts a large concentration of maritime temperate glaciers that are highly sensitive to climate change. However, persistent cloud cover, seasonal snow, and supraglacial debris complicate consistent long-term glacier mapping, while the use of static glacier boundaries may introduce temporal mismatches in altimetry-based glacier mass-change estimates. In this study, we developed a multi-source data-fusion framework on Google Earth Engine (GEE) to reconstruct glacier-area changes in the SETP from 2000 to 2025 at five-year intervals and 30 m spatial resolution. Random Forest classifiers were used to integrate Landsat and Sentinel-2 optical imagery, Sentinel-1 synthetic-aperture-radar data, and NASADEM-derived topographic information, supporting glacier delineation under complex surface and atmospheric conditions. The reconstructed glacier area decreased from 8,083 ± 664 km2 in 2000 to 6,228 ± 572 km2 in 2025, corresponding to a cumulative loss of 22.9 ± 3.6% and a mean loss rate of 80.51 ± 10.51 km2 yr−1. The mean area-loss rates were 51.31 ± 6.51 km2 yr−1 during 2000–2010 and 92.99 ± 15.55 km2 yr−1 during 2010–2025, indicating a higher average loss rate in the later period. By combining satellite-altimetry-derived elevation changes from ICESat, CryoSat-2, and ICESat-2 with the reconstructed time-varying glacier areas, we estimated a mean glacier mass-change rate of −6.51 ± 1.22 Gt yr−1 during 2003–2022. Compared with using a fixed 2003 glacier area, the time-varying-area calculation reduced the estimated mass-loss magnitude by 0.63 Gt yr−1, equivalent to 8.8% of the fixed-area estimate. These results indicate that incorporating time-varying glacier areas can reduce temporal mismatch in altimetry-based mass-change estimation and improve the temporal consistency of regional glacier mass-change assessments.

title: Test-Time Computing for Referring Multimodal Large Language Models
Event-Guided Decomposition from a Long-Exposure Nighttime Snapshot into Video Sequence
Multi-View Optimal Transport for Multi-View Crowd Localization and Tracking
Learning from Automatic 3D Gaussian Splatting Edits for Online Bayesian Scene Change Detection
abstract: Online scene change detection requires integrating incoming observations to determine which regions have changed relative to a reference scene. We update change beliefs as new images arrive using generalised Bayesian evidence fusion. However, the prior probability of change and evidence models are unknown beforehand, and numerical Bayesian inference can be costly. We address these challenges by learning offline from automatic edits to a reference 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) model. These edits generate labelled training views without manual annotations. Together with unchanged reference observations, they provide supervision for learning scene-specific evidence models and estimating the effective pixel prior and response statistics. Online prediction combines current evidence with historical support, while closed-form local Bayes factors, parameterized by the learned response statistics, update an accumulated 3D Gaussian field. Object-guided refinement produces the final change masks. Our method achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on PASLCD and CCS3D, with $67.64\%$ and $75.82\%$ mIoU, respectively. On PASLCD, the complete pipeline runs at $17.2$\,FPS over complete query sequences, the fastest among the evaluated online methods.

title: Efficient SAM3 Adaptation for Multi-Class Semantic Segmentation via Dense Competitive Representations
abstract: The Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM3) has achieved significant progress in Promptable Concept Segmentation (PCS) by processing short noun phrases to generate segmentation masks with unique instance identifiers. While SAM3 excels at single-concept segmentation, it falls short in complex, real-world environments where multiple concepts must be segmented simultaneously. In particular, SAM3 typically fails to simultaneously process concepts with semantic overlap, leading to semantic misclassifications and redundant mask predictions. Moreover, as the number of concepts increases, the independent inference paradigm introduces prohibitive inference latency. To address these limitations, we propose the Dense Competitive Representations SAM (DCR-SAM) framework. By decoupling cross-modal interactions, the proposed method alleviates the inference latency. To resolve semantic misclassifications, DCR-SAM dynamically aligns textual concepts with visual representations and incorporates a dense competition head to enforce explicit inter-class competition. Furthermore, a learnable background token is applied to absorb non-target objects dynamically. These mechanisms effectively suppress overlapping predictions and generate high-fidelity masks. Extensive experimental evaluations across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed framework: (1) achieves a 2.3% $\sim$ 10.7% performance improvement over state-of-the-art methods, (2) delivers a 33$\times$ inference speedup compared to the native SAM3, and (3) exhibits strong robustness across diverse scenarios.
